implementation_notes: Ruby evaluates the whole right-hand side before making any assignment (parallel assignment), so `a, b = b, a` is the exchange and needs no temporary; it is documented in the assignment reference and in the classic tutorial as the way to swap, and it works for locals, instance variables and array elements. Because ivar assignment binds a reference and cannot itself raise, the classic C++ structure (member swap, ADL, noexcept) is replaced by a small method that exchanges the two ivars - the only failure modes are a writer method (attr_writer, a custom setter, FrozenError on a frozen receiver) and the fact that the two assignments are not atomic. For lists, `ary[i], ary[j] = ary[j], ary[i]` is the same parallel assignment.
code_sketch:
class Cache
  def initialize(state) = (@state = state)

  def swap_state(other)            # exchange the representation: cannot raise
    mine = @state
    @state = other.state
    other.state = mine
  end

  protected
  attr_accessor :state             # protected writer, not a public setter
end
pitfalls: A public writer (attr_accessor, a custom setter) runs arbitrary code and can raise or validate; swap the ivars from inside the class instead of through the public setter when the exchange must not fail.
Frozen objects raise FrozenError on instance-variable assignment, so a swap helper can fail on a frozen receiver even though plain assignment cannot raise.

Two ivars or references are not exchanged atomically: another thread or a Fiber can observe the intermediate state where both refer to the same object; publish through one reference or guard shared state with a Mutex.

Parallel assignment still evaluates the left-hand-side targets after the right-hand side (and assigns left to right), so mixing a swap with index expressions such as `i, ary[i] = ary[i], 7` has surprising results - keep the exchange to plain variables.
